Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum: Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum stands solemnly in historic Ba Dinh Square, where Uncle Ho read the Declaration of Independence that gave birth to the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. Its architecture is deeply Vietnamese and combines precious materials from every region of the country, making it a sacred symbol of reverence and national unity.

Standing on the bank of the Red River with a history of more than 500 years, Bat Trang is one of the oldest and most famous cradles of ceramics in Vietnam. In the skilled hands of its artisans, plain lumps of clay become exquisite works with a distinctive glaze, serving everyday life while carrying artistic value that reaches the world.

The folk-painting village of Dong Ho is famous for its rustic woodblock prints, which vividly reflect the labor, customs and simple hopes of the ancient Vietnamese. What gives Dong Ho paintings their lasting vitality is the glittering dó paper coated with shell powder and a palette made entirely from nature: pagoda-tree flowers, indigo leaves, bamboo charcoal and red pebbles.

Founded in 1149 under King Ly Anh Tong, Van Don was the first international seaport of Dai Viet and one of its busiest for centuries. Set among the majestic islands of Bai Tu Long Bay, it was once the bridge that carried Vietnamese ceramics and silk out to the open sea, marking an era of prosperous openness.

Right beside the scenic Tam Coc – Bich Dong, the Van Lam lace embroidery village is more than 700 years old and famed for fine, lively needlework. From tablecloths and landscape pictures to artistic costumes, every piece here crystallizes the patience, skill and deep aesthetic taste of the artisans of the old capital.

The coastal land of Nga Son has long been known for its vast sedge fields and centuries-old tradition of mat weaving. Thanks to supple, fine sedge fibers, firm weaving techniques and lasting dyes, Nga Son sedge mats are not only a familiar item in every Vietnamese home but also a source of pride for the land of Thanh.

The Lam River (Lam Giang) winds through the land of Nghe, rich in talent and sacred energy, witnessing countless ups and downs of history and nurturing a steadfast, studious character in its people. From the humble ví and giặm folk songs to the changing life along its banks today, Lam Giang remains a symbol of the enduring vitality and aspiration of Central Vietnam.

The conical-hat village of Ba Don has been bound to the people along the Gianh River for generations, where each hat is stitched with care from young palm leaves, thinly shaved bamboo hoops and fine thread. More than a familiar shelter from sun and rain, the graceful, durable Ba Don hat carries the simple charm of the land of Lao winds and white sand.

The Thuy Xuan incense village is known for its long-standing incense making in Hue, famous for the gentle, pure fragrance of natural ingredients. It also attracts visitors from near and far with the dazzling sight of multicolored incense stick bundles in green, red, purple and yellow, spread like flowers under the sun of the old capital.

Tien Sa is an important seaport area of Da Nang, set beside the picturesque Da Nang Bay and tied to the city's strategic position in sea trade. Today Tien Sa Port is one of the largest ports in Central Vietnam, playing a key role in import–export activity and connecting goods with the world.

Thanh Ha pottery village is a long-established craft village in Hoi An, formed in the 16th century and originating from Thanh Chiem village. It flourished in the 16th–17th centuries, its characteristic reddish-brown unglazed pottery being regarded as a precious local product offered to the king. Today the village still preserves its handmade techniques and has become an attractive cultural tourism destination in Hoi An.

Known as the "kingdom of garlic", Ly Son island is famous for garlic grown in red basalt soil mixed with white coral sand along the coast. Thanks to its special soil and the painstaking care of farmers on this frontline island, Ly Son garlic has small, glossy white cloves, a mild strong aroma and a gentle spiciness that few places can match.

Binh Dinh has long been called the land of "martial arts and literature", famous for its martial tradition and the indomitable spirit of Central Vietnam. It is the cradle of Binh Dinh traditional martial arts, tied to the Tay Son movement and the name of the commoner hero Quang Trung – Nguyen Hue. Today these martial arts are a distinctive cultural heritage that shapes the identity of Binh Dinh.

The harvesting and processing of bird's nest in Khanh Hoa has existed for hundreds of years, tied to the precipitous island caves off Nha Trang. Blessed by nature with nutritious island swiftlet nests and by the workers' painstaking harvesting and processing techniques, Nha Trang bird's nest has long been a precious delicacy and a pride of the Tram incense land.

Over hundreds of years, Bau Truc pottery has been nurtured and preserved in the traditional village of the same name in Phuoc Dan town, Ninh Phuoc district, Ninh Thuan province. Shaped entirely by hand without a potter's wheel and fired in the open air, it is one of the oldest Cham pottery villages in Southeast Asia – a living museum keeping the precious cultural values of the Cham people.

To this day Phan Thiet fish sauce keeps its pure traditional flavor, made from fresh anchovies and sea salt fermented in the barrel, despite more than 300 years of ups and downs in the craft village. With its characteristic cockroach-wing brown color, savory taste and rich sweet aftertaste, Phan Thiet fish sauce has become a familiar seasoning in every Vietnamese family kitchen.

The An Ngai rice paper village (Long Dien district) has a history of more than a hundred years and is recognized as a National Intangible Cultural Heritage. Made from good rice mixed in the proper ratio, the sheets are coated by hand over a glowing fire and dried evenly on bamboo racks in the seaside sun and wind, giving a simple, chewy and fragrant flavor tied to local food life.

Cellophane-paper lanterns – a traditional beauty tied to the full-moon seasons of childhood memories – are still kept alive by the skilled hands of artisans in Saigon's famous Phu Binh lantern village. Curved bamboo frames, vivid cellophane paper and lively hand-painted strokes have lit up the warm Mid-Autumn atmosphere for generations.

Thoi Son Islet (Con Lan) lies in the lower Tien River and is one of the islets of the famed Mekong "four sacred creatures" – Dragon, Unicorn, Turtle and Phoenix. With a large area of up to 50 hectares, orchards heavy with fruit and a gentle river-life rhythm, Thoi Son is regarded by locals as a precious jewel.

To mention the coconut land of Ben Tre is to mention rich coconut candies, fragrant with fresh coconut cream and chewy malt syrup. Born in the mid-20th century, the craft has gone through many changes and created new flavors while keeping the sweet, honest character of the orchard people.

Tra Cuon banh tet is one of Tra Vinh's famous specialties, unforgettable after one bite thanks to the lush green of katuk leaves blended with sticky rice, mung beans, fatty pork and salted egg yolk. To make a fragrant, tasty cake, the maker must be meticulous from choosing ingredients and wrapping to cooking – each cake is like a work of art showing the skill and dedication of its artisan.

The Vung Thom pia cake village began with Chinese-origin families in the two villages of Phuoc Tam and Phu No, starting from Cong Lap Thanh bakery of Mr. Au Minh Xuong and spreading to many famous bakeries such as Thuan Thanh, Tan Hung, My Hiep Thanh, Tao Thanh... Thanks to the distinctive nutty flavor of mung beans, durian and salted egg yolk, pia cake has become a specialty that makes Soc Trang's culinary brand.

Bac Lieu is a poetic land famous for many sights such as the Bac Lieu Playboy's Mansion, Xiem Can Pagoda and the ancient longan garden, along with its traditional salt-making craft, a National Intangible Cultural Heritage. The salt fields gleaming white under the sun, together with the image of salt farmers hard at work, form a simple picture that leaves many unforgettable impressions.

In the southernmost land of the Fatherland, where mangrove forests meet the sea, ecological shrimp farming under the mangrove canopy has become Ca Mau's main livelihood and signature. Shrimp ponds stretching through vast greenery not only provide high-quality seafood for the world but also show the sustainable, nature-friendly way of life of the people of Cape Ca Mau.

Thanks to calm seas, clear blue water and plankton-rich waters, the pearl island of Phu Quoc is an ideal place for high-quality pearl culture. Combining modern culture techniques with meticulous craftsmanship, Phu Quoc pearls, glittering with natural mother-of-pearl, have become the island's luxurious gift from the sea.

Formed in the early 20th century, Cai Rang floating market is where Mekong people gather to trade goods and specialties of the Mekong Delta right on the water. With a scene of busy boats and unique "cây bẹo" poles hung with goods from the early dawn, Cai Rang floating market is always a familiar stop on any itinerary exploring Can Tho.

The Tan Chau silk-weaving village was once famous throughout Cochinchina for its renowned My A silk, notable for its glossy jet-black color dyed with natural mac nua fruit. After dozens of painstaking weaving, dyeing and sun-drying steps, Tan Chau silk is soft, cool and durable – a treasured heritage of the upper Tien River region.

Beside the fertile Tien River with a history of more than 100 years, the Sa Dec flower village is one of the largest ornamental-flower growers in the Mekong Delta. Its unique feature is flower beds raised above the water, where farmers paddle boats to tend thousands of species blooming brilliantly all year round, especially lively when spring comes.

The Binh An drum-making village (Tan Tru district) has a history of nearly 200 years and is famous throughout the Mekong region for buffalo-hide, jackfruit-wood drums with resonant, warm sound. To make a durable, beautiful drum, the artisan goes through many elaborate steps from bending the body and tanning hide to stretching the head and tuning the sound, keeping alive the drums of Southern festivals.

To mention Tay Ninh is to mention Trang Bang dew-dried rice paper – a unique specialty coated in two layers, lightly grilled until puffy, then dried in the night dew to reach just the right softness. Its mild saltiness and the scent of new rice, when rolled with boiled pork and fresh wild herbs, give the local cuisine an irresistible appeal.

With a history of more than 300 years, the Buu Long stone carving craft (Bien Hoa, Dong Nai) is tied to the Hakka Chinese community who migrated to this land. Skilled workers craft many exquisite products such as stone statues, mythical creatures, worship items and household objects. Over generations, Buu Long stone carving has become a distinctive handicraft culture of Dong Nai.

The Southern Central Highlands appear majestic with rolling red basalt hills, waterfalls tossing white spray and the Dak Nong UNESCO Global Geopark. The land still keeps the echo of gongs, heroic epics and the resolute, generous spirit of the ethnic peoples in their journey of conquering nature.

In the Langbiang plateau, misty all year round, greenhouses stretching across the hillsides have become the signature image of Da Lat's high-tech agriculture. Thanks to the mild climate and modern farming techniques, Da Lat has become a "kingdom" of fresh flowers, strawberries and clean vegetables, and at night it glitters like a "capital of light".

Known as the "coffee capital of Vietnam", Buon Ma Thuot has fertile red basalt soil and an ideal climate for vast Robusta coffee plantations. Its beans carry a rich aroma, a bold bitterness and a deep aftertaste, shaping Vietnamese coffee culture and taking the country's agricultural brand to the world.

Folk wood statues are among the most unique sculptural arts of the Jrai people in the Northern Central Highlands. With just an axe, a crude knife and free-flowing strokes that follow no mold, the artisan breathes life into every piece of forest wood to portray the life, feelings and deep spiritual world of the village.

The traditional brocade weaving of the Ba Na, Xo Dang and Gie Trieng peoples in Kon Tum is a beautiful blend of handcraft technique and the artistic soul of Central Highlands women. On rustic looms, threads dyed with natural colors interlace into colorful geometric patterns, birds, animals and communal houses, telling the cultural story of the great forest.

Quang Tri Citadel is a tragic historical witness tied to the 81 days and nights of resolute fighting in the summer of 1972. Through storms of bombs and bullets and many upheavals of the times, the sacred land beside the Thach Han River is now lush green, an enduring symbol of patriotism, noble sacrifice and the longing for peace.

Nam Dan soybean sauce is a rustic dipping sauce famous in Nghe An, made from humble ingredients: soybeans, corn or sticky rice, white salt and clean water. Thanks to painstaking mold fermentation and months of natural sun-drying, each batch is smooth and thick, with a distinctive aroma and a harmonious mild sweetness, steeped in the flavor of Uncle Ho's homeland.

Rượu cần (jar wine) is a traditional drink indispensable at festivals, housewarmings and welcoming honored guests among the Muong people of Muong Vang (Lac Son, Hoa Binh). Brewed from upland sticky rice and secret wild-leaf yeast in ancient clay jars, it has a gentle sweetness and a warm, slightly spicy kick, a bond of kinship around the stilt-house fire.

The Pieu scarf is the pride and symbol of the skill and diligence of Thai women in Son La. On a plain indigo cloth, vivid geometric patterns and motifs are embroidered entirely by hand from the reverse side of the fabric, not only adorning the charm of Northwestern girls but also carrying deep meaning in spiritual life.

Set in the cool green valley of Tam Duong district, the Binh Lu glass-noodle village is famous for crystal-clear, chewy noodles with the mild scent of arrowroot grown on high fields. Made from pure spring water and dried naturally on bamboo racks spread throughout the village, Binh Lu noodles have become a quintessential specialty of the Northwest mountains.

The highland market of the Northwest is not only a place to exchange farm produce, brocade or tools but also a colorful cultural space for ethnic minority communities. In the drifting morning mist, the sound of the khen pipe calling friends, brocade skirts and shirts mingle with the aroma of thang co and corn wine to form a vivid and captivating highland scene.

In the majestic Dong Van rock plateau, the Lung Tam linen weaving cooperative (Quan Ba) is where Hmong women keep the traditional linen craft alive through dozens of entirely handmade steps. From stripping flax bark, spinning thread and weaving cloth to beeswax drawing and natural indigo dyeing, each piece of linen has a rustic, durable beauty rich in the identity of the far north.

The Phuc Sen blacksmith village (Quang Hoa district) of the Nung An people has a history of more than 300 years and is famous nationwide for sharp, super-durable knives, scissors and farm tools. The smiths here still keep the handmade steel-tempering technique, judging by the keen sense of fire color and the sound of the hammer, creating the renowned Phuc Sen knife brand.

Standing tall on a mountaintop in Tam Thanh ward (Lang Son city), Vong Phu Rock takes the shape of a mother holding her child gazing into the distance, tied to the moving legend of steadfast fidelity. Amid the windswept border clouds, the thousand-year-old stone standing firm against storms has also become a symbol of the resolute, enduring spirit of the people of Lang Son.

The Chu noodle village of Thu Duong (Luc Ngan district) is famous for snow-white, chewy rice noodles that do not break when cooked. The secret behind Chu noodles' fame lies in the local Bao Thai Hong rice variety, sweet well water and the skilled hands of people in the Northern midlands who coat, cut and sun-dry the sheets.

Known as the "number one famous tea", the Tan Cuong tea region impresses with lush green tea hills curving like inverted bowls at the foot of the Tam Dao range. Thanks to its special climate and soil and the masterful handmade tea-roasting of local people, Tan Cuong tea has a delicate young-rice-flake fragrance, a mild astringency and an unforgettable deep sweet aftertaste.
